questions.question: Design a parking lot system. Walk me through your approach.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to decompose a real-world system into cohesive classes and identify correct relationships (composition, inheritance, aggregation).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating a single God class that does everything or missing key entities like ParkingTicket, leading to difficulty tracking vehicle entry/exit times.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention explicit concurrency handling for spot assignment and justify each design pattern choice with the specific problem it solves in this domain.

questions.direct_answer: A parking lot system needs ParkingLot (manages floors), ParkingFloor (manages spots), ParkingSpot (tracks occupancy), Vehicle hierarchy (Car, Motorcycle, Truck), ParkingTicket (entry/exit tracking), and FeeCalculator (pricing logic). Use Singleton for ParkingLot, Strategy for fee calculation, and Factory for vehicle creation.

items: ParkingLot: Singleton, holds List<ParkingFloor>, find spot, issue/process ticket
ParkingFloor: holds Map<String, ParkingSpot>, methods for available spots by type
ParkingSpot: spot ID, type enum, occupied flag, park/vacate methods
Vehicle: abstract class with licensePlate, VehicleType; Car/Motorcycle/Truck subclasses
ParkingTicket: generated on entry, tracks vehicle, spot, entry time
FeeCalculator: Strategy pattern for different pricing (hourly, flat)
DisplayBoard: Observer pattern to show availability

answer_sections.content: For a parking lot design, I start by identifying entities. The physical objects: ParkingLot, ParkingFloor, ParkingSpot. The actors: Vehicle (abstract) with Car, Motorcycle, Truck subclasses. The transactional objects: ParkingTicket issued on entry, Payment on exit. The services: FeeCalculator. ParkingLot is a Singleton since there's one. ParkingFloor has a map of spots keyed by spot ID for O(1) lookup. ParkingSpot tracks its occupancy and has a canPark() method that checks if the vehicle type fits. On entry: find available spot → park vehicle → issue ticket. On exit: calculate fee → process payment → free spot → mark ticket paid. FeeCalculator uses the Strategy pattern so I can swap in different pricing without changing ParkingLot.

How would you add support for electric vehicle charging spots?

sections.title: Designing a Parking Lot — The Approach
sections.content:
**Low-Level Design (LLD)** means turning a real-world problem into **classes**, their **fields**, and the **relationships** between them. The parking lot is the classic warm-up because it exercises almost every OOP idea at once: inheritance, composition, enums, and a couple of design patterns.

The trick is to find the **nouns** (they become classes) and the **verbs** (they become methods). Nouns here: parking lot, floor, spot, vehicle, ticket, fee. Verbs: park, unpark, calculate fee.

The single most important modelling decision: a **ParkingLot HAS-A list of ParkingFloors**, each **floor HAS-A list of ParkingSpots** (composition), while **Car, Motorcycle, Truck IS-A Vehicle** (inheritance). Get that split right and the rest follows.

sections.title: Approach in 5 Steps
sections.content:
| Step | What you do | Output |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Clarify | Ask: multiple floors? vehicle types? hourly pricing? | Scope is fixed |
| 2. Find entities | Nouns → `ParkingLot`, `ParkingFloor`, `ParkingSpot`, `Vehicle`, `ParkingTicket`, `FeeCalculator` | Candidate classes |
| 3. Assign responsibility | One job per class (SRP): spot tracks occupancy, lot finds spots | Cohesive classes |
| 4. Map relationships | Lot →* Floor →* Spot (composition); Car/Truck → Vehicle (inheritance) | Class diagram |
| 5. Add patterns | Strategy for fees, Factory for vehicles, Singleton for the lot | Extensible design |

Start with steps 1–4; only reach for patterns in step 5 when they solve a real problem.

sections.title: Java Skeleton — Core Classes
Class Relationships
sections.content:
```mermaid
classDiagram
    class ParkingLot
    class ParkingFloor
    class ParkingSpot
    class Vehicle
    class Car
    class Truck
    class ParkingTicket
    class FeeCalculator
    ParkingLot "1" *-- "*" ParkingFloor : has
    ParkingFloor "1" *-- "*" ParkingSpot : has
    Vehicle <|-- Car
    Vehicle <|-- Truck
    ParkingSpot --> Vehicle : holds
    ParkingLot --> FeeCalculator : uses
    ParkingLot ..> ParkingTicket : issues
```
*Filled diamond (`*--`) = composition (the part dies with the whole); hollow triangle (`<|--`) = inheritance.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **The God class** — one `ParkingLotManager` doing spots, tickets, and fees. Split by responsibility (SRP) so each class has one reason to change.
- **Forgetting the ParkingTicket** — without a ticket capturing entry time, you can't compute the fee on exit. The ticket is the contract between customer and system.
- **if-else on vehicle type** — `if (type == CAR) ... else if (type == TRUCK)` scattered everywhere. Use polymorphism (`requiredSize()`) so a new type is one new class.
- **Ignoring concurrency** — two gates can grab the same spot. A `synchronized` claim on the spot prevents double-booking.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Find nouns → classes, verbs → methods.** Lot, Floor, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket, FeeCalculator.
- **Composition for structure** (`ParkingLot` HAS-A floors), **inheritance for vehicles** (`Car` IS-A `Vehicle`).
- **Enums** (`VehicleType`, `SpotSize`) beat String constants for type safety.
- **Patterns last**: Strategy (fees), Factory (vehicles), Singleton (the lot) — each for a real reason.
- **Narrate the flow**: entry → find spot → park → issue ticket; exit → fee → pay → free spot.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
I'd start by clarifying scope — multiple floors, what vehicle types, and whether pricing is hourly. Then I find the nouns in the problem, because nouns usually become classes. Here that's ParkingLot, ParkingFloor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, ParkingTicket, and a FeeCalculator. The verbs — park, unpark, calculate fee — become the methods.

The most important modelling decision is the relationships. A ParkingLot has a list of floors, and each floor has a list of spots — that's composition, because a spot can't exist without its floor. Vehicles are different: Car, Motorcycle, and Truck all inherit from an abstract Vehicle class, because each one is-a vehicle. I'd give Vehicle an abstract method like requiredSize so each subclass declares what spot it needs, instead of writing if-else chains on the type.

For the flow: on entry, the lot searches floors for a free spot that fits, marks it occupied, and issues a ParkingTicket that records the vehicle, the spot, and the entry time. On exit, the customer hands back the ticket, the FeeCalculator works out the charge from the duration, payment is taken, and the spot is freed.

Then I'd layer in patterns where they earn their place: Strategy for the FeeCalculator so pricing rules can change without touching the lot, Factory for creating vehicles, and Singleton for the lot since there's only one. I'd also mention that spot assignment must be thread-safe, since multiple gates operate at once — a synchronized claim on the spot stops two cars taking the same place. That shows I'm thinking about behaviour, not just structure.

questions.question: How does the fee calculation work in your parking lot design?

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Strategy pattern and ability to isolate business logic that changes frequently from stable system structure.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Hardcoding fee calculation directly in ParkingLot or ParkingTicket classes, making it impossible to change pricing rules without modifying core code.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how Strategy enables A/B testing different pricing models in production by simply swapping the calculator instance at runtime.

questions.direct_answer: Fee calculation uses the Strategy pattern. Define a FeeCalculator interface with calculateFee(ParkingTicket ticket) method. Concrete implementations like HourlyFeeCalculator, FlatRateFeeCalculator, and VehicleTypeFeeCalculator contain the pricing logic. ParkingLot holds a FeeCalculator reference and delegates fee computation to it.

answer_sections.content: For fee calculation, I use the Strategy pattern. I define a FeeCalculator interface with a single calculate() method that takes a ParkingTicket (which has entry time, vehicle type, spot type). HourlyFeeCalculator multiplies hours parked by the hourly rate for that vehicle type. FlatRateFeeCalculator returns a flat fee. WeekendPricingCalculator might apply different rates on weekends. ParkingLot holds a FeeCalculator reference — at runtime, you can swap the strategy without changing ParkingLot code. This aligns with OCP: adding a new pricing model means adding a new class, not modifying existing ones. BigDecimal for money — never float or double for currency calculations.

How would you handle free parking for the first 30 minutes?

FlatRateFeeCalculator: returns a fixed fee regardless of time

production trap: never use float or double for money calculations. Always use BigDecimal. Floating-point arithmetic introduces rounding errors that compound in financial systems.

sections.title: Fee Calculation with the Strategy Pattern
sections.content:
Fee rules change constantly — hourly, flat, weekend, vehicle-based — but the core parking logic almost never changes. When one part changes and another doesn't, you separate them. That's the **Strategy pattern**: define a `FeeCalculator` **interface** with one method, then provide a class per pricing rule.

The `ParkingLot` holds a `FeeCalculator` reference but never knows which concrete one it is. This is the **Open/Closed Principle** — adding `WeekendFeeCalculator` is a *new class*, not an edit to `ParkingLot`.

sections.title: Without Strategy — pricing hard-wired into the lot
With Strategy — each rule is its own class
Strategy Structure
sections.content:
```mermaid
classDiagram
    class FeeCalculator {
        <<interface>>
        +calculate(ticket, exit) BigDecimal
    }
    class HourlyFeeCalculator
    class FlatRateFeeCalculator
    class WeekendFeeCalculator
    class ParkingLot
    FeeCalculator <|.. HourlyFeeCalculator
    FeeCalculator <|.. FlatRateFeeCalculator
    FeeCalculator <|.. WeekendFeeCalculator
    ParkingLot --> FeeCalculator : delegates
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `double` for money** — floating point rounds wrong. Always `BigDecimal` for currency.
- **Fee logic inside `ParkingTicket`** — the ticket is a dumb data holder; algorithms live in the calculator (SRP).
- **Calling `LocalDateTime.now()` inside the calculator** — pass `exit` in so the method is testable with fixed times.
- **A switch on pricing mode** — that's the anti-pattern Strategy removes; each branch should be a class.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Strategy** = one `FeeCalculator` interface, many implementations, swappable at runtime.
- **Open/Closed**: new pricing rule = new class, no edit to `ParkingLot`.
- **BigDecimal**, never `double`/`float`, for any money calculation.
- **Pass exit time in** so fees are deterministic and unit-testable.
- The lot **delegates** to the strategy — it never knows the concrete rule.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Fee calculation is the classic place to use the Strategy pattern, because pricing rules change a lot while the parking logic stays the same. I'd define a FeeCalculator interface with a single method — calculate, taking the ticket and an exit time and returning the amount. Then each pricing rule becomes its own class: HourlyFeeCalculator multiplies the parked hours by an hourly rate, FlatRateFeeCalculator returns a fixed amount, WeekendFeeCalculator uses a cheaper rate.

The ParkingLot just holds a FeeCalculator reference and delegates to it — it never knows which concrete strategy is active. That's the power of it: when the business wants surge pricing during an event, I write a new SurgePricingCalculator and inject it, and I don't touch ParkingLot or ParkingTicket at all. That's the Open/Closed Principle — open for extension, closed for modification.

Two details that show production awareness. First, I'd use BigDecimal for the money, never double or float, because floating point introduces rounding errors that compound in financial systems. Second, I'd pass the exit time into the method rather than calling now inside it, so the calculation is deterministic and I can unit-test it with a fixed clock.

The mistake I'd call out is putting an if-else or switch on the pricing mode directly inside ParkingLot. Every new rule then means editing and retesting that method. With Strategy, a new rule is just a new class — that's the whole point.

questions.question: How would you extend the parking lot design for multiple locations?

interviewer_intent.testing: Extensibility thinking—can the candidate evolve a design to handle new requirements without breaking existing abstractions or creating tight coupling.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to retrofit ParkingLot as a multi-location entity, violating Single Responsibility Principle and creating a tangled design.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss how the network layer could use the Composite pattern to treat single lots and lot collections uniformly, enabling recursive aggregation.

questions.direct_answer: Introduce a ParkingLotNetwork or ParkingManagementSystem class that aggregates multiple ParkingLot instances. Each ParkingLot remains an independent unit with its own floors and spots. The network layer provides cross-location operations like findNearestAvailableSpot(Location userLocation) or getTotalOccupancyAcrossAllLots().

answer_sections.content: If there are multiple locations, I introduce a ParkingLotNetwork class. Each ParkingLot is still a complete, independent unit. ParkingLotNetwork holds a List<ParkingLot> and has methods like findNearestLotWithAvailability(Location, VehicleType). This doesn't require changing the existing ParkingLot class at all — OCP in action. For cross-lot operations, ParkingLotNetwork can aggregate availability across all lots or route vehicles to the best option based on proximity. I'd also extract an IParkingLot interface that both ParkingLot and ParkingLotNetwork implement — then calling code works with either one. This follows the Composite design pattern — individual lots and the network both implement the same interface.

follow_up_questions: What design pattern are you applying when ParkingLotNetwork and ParkingLot share an interface?
How would you implement a 'find nearest lot' algorithm?

sections.title: Scaling to Multiple Locations
sections.content:
When the interviewer says *"now support multiple lots"*, the wrong move is to bolt location logic onto `ParkingLot`. The right move is to add a new layer **above** it: a `ParkingLotNetwork` that **aggregates** independent `ParkingLot` instances.

Each lot stays exactly as it was — that's the **Open/Closed Principle** in action. The network adds cross-location operations like *find the nearest lot with a free spot*. Extract a shared `IParkingLot` interface and you've got the **Composite pattern**: callers treat a single lot and the whole network the same way.

sections.title: Java Skeleton — Network Layer
Composite Layering
sections.content:
```mermaid
classDiagram
    class IParkingLot {
        <<interface>>
        +park(v) Optional
        +availableCount() int
    }
    class ParkingLot
    class ParkingLotNetwork
    IParkingLot <|.. ParkingLot
    IParkingLot <|.. ParkingLotNetwork
    ParkingLotNetwork "1" o-- "*" ParkingLot : aggregates
```
*Both implement `IParkingLot`, so callers don't care if they hold one lot or many.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Adding a `neighbors` list to `ParkingLot`** — creates circular references and makes each lot know about others. Coordination belongs in the network layer.
- **Duplicating spot-search logic** in the network — it should *delegate* to each lot, not re-implement parking (DRY).
- **No lot identity** — each lot needs an id and `GeoLocation`, or you can't route or report per-lot.
- **Modifying `ParkingLot`** at all — if you're editing it, you've missed the Open/Closed point.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Add a `ParkingLotNetwork` **above** existing lots — don't modify `ParkingLot` (Open/Closed).
- **Aggregation, not inheritance**: the network *contains* lots.
- A shared `IParkingLot` interface gives you the **Composite pattern**.
- The network **delegates** spot search and **aggregates** results (availability, revenue).
- Each lot carries an id + `GeoLocation` so the network can route by proximity.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The clean way to support multiple locations is to add a new layer above the existing design rather than changing the lot itself. I'd create a ParkingLotNetwork class that holds a collection of ParkingLot instances — usually a map keyed by lot id. Each individual lot stays exactly as it was, with its own floors and spots. That's the Open/Closed Principle: I'm extending the system by adding a class, not modifying working code.

The network is where cross-location features live. For finding the nearest lot with a free spot, the network takes the user's location, filters to lots that have availability, and picks the one with the smallest distance. For total occupancy, it just streams over all lots and sums their counts. The key idea is that the network coordinates and aggregates, but the actual parking logic stays inside ParkingLot where it belongs.

To make it really clean, I'd extract an IParkingLot interface with the common operations, and have both ParkingLot and ParkingLotNetwork implement it. Now calling code can talk to either one without knowing whether it's a single lot or a whole network — that's the Composite pattern.

The mistake I'd avoid is adding a neighbors list directly onto ParkingLot. That makes every lot aware of the others, creates circular dependencies, and violates single responsibility. Each lot should only know about its own floors and spots; the network handles everything that spans locations. In a real system, each lot could even be its own microservice with the network acting as an API gateway routing by geography.

questions.question: What design patterns did you apply in the parking lot design and why?

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of design pattern knowledge and ability to justify pattern choices with concrete benefits specific to the parking lot domain.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing patterns without explaining why they're needed or applying them where simpler solutions would suffice, showing pattern obsession over pragmatism.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast each pattern with the problem it solves—explain what would break or become unmaintainable without the pattern.

questions.direct_answer: Singleton ensures one ParkingLot instance system-wide. Strategy decouples fee calculation from parking logic, allowing runtime swaps. Observer updates DisplayBoards when spot status changes without tight coupling. Factory Method creates Vehicle subclasses, centralizing instantiation. Builder constructs complex ParkingTicket objects with optional fields cleanly.

answer_sections.content: I applied several patterns deliberately. Singleton for ParkingLot — there's one, and having multiple instances would be a bug. Strategy for FeeCalculator — pricing rules change without requiring changes to ParkingLot. Observer for the DisplayBoard — when a ParkingSpot's occupancy changes, it notifies the DisplayBoard to update availability counts; this decouples spot management from display. Factory Method for Vehicle creation — VehicleFactory.create(VehicleType.CAR) returns the right subclass without the caller knowing the exact type. Builder for ParkingTicket — it has many optional fields (entryTime, vehicle, spot, status) and Builder makes construction readable. Each pattern was applied to solve a specific design problem, not just to use patterns.

sections.title: Patterns as Problem–Solution Pairs
sections.content:
Design patterns aren't decoration — each one removes a *specific* maintenance pain. In the parking lot, five patterns each solve one problem:

- **Singleton** — exactly one `ParkingLot` coordinating shared spots.
- **Strategy** — pluggable `FeeCalculator` so pricing changes don't touch parking logic.
- **Observer** — `DisplayBoard`s update when a spot changes, without the spot knowing the board.
- **Factory** — one place decides which `Vehicle` subclass to build.
- **Builder** — readable construction of a `ParkingTicket` with optional fields.

The interviewer wants the *problem* first, then the pattern name — never the reverse.

sections.title: Java Skeleton — Patterns Together
Where Each Pattern Sits
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB LOT["ParkingLot
(Singleton)"] FEE["FeeCalculator
(Strategy)"] OBS["DisplayBoard
(Observer)"] FAC["VehicleFactory
(Factory)"] TKT["ParkingTicket
(Builder)"] LOT --> FEE LOT --> OBS LOT --> FAC LOT --> TKT ```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Pattern for pattern's sake** — a Factory for a two-class hierarchy adds noise. Use it only when creation logic is real.
- **Singleton on the wrong thing** — `ParkingSpot` should be thousands of instances, not a Singleton. Singleton is for one shared coordinator.
- **Observer without unregister** — boards never removed = memory leak. Always provide `removeObserver`.
- **Listing patterns with no justification** — say the problem ("pricing changes often") *then* the pattern ("so Strategy").

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Singleton** → one shared `ParkingLot`; prevents inconsistent spot state.
- **Strategy** → swap pricing without editing the lot (Open/Closed).
- **Observer** → decouple spot changes from display boards.
- **Factory** → centralize `Vehicle` creation; no scattered `new`.
- **Builder** → readable tickets with many optional fields.
- Always pair **problem → pattern**, and skip patterns that don't earn their place.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
I'd name five patterns, but the important thing is tying each one to the problem it solves. First, Singleton for ParkingLot — there's one physical lot, and multiple instances would mean two objects both thinking the same spot is free, so I make the constructor private and expose a getInstance. Second, Strategy for fee calculation, because pricing rules change far more often than parking logic — I inject a FeeCalculator interface so adding weekend pricing is a new class, not an edit to the lot. That's Open/Closed.

Third, Observer for the display boards. When a spot's occupancy changes, several boards need updating. Instead of the spot calling each board directly, boards register as observers and get notified — that keeps the spot decoupled from the display. Fourth, Factory Method for vehicles. When I parse a type string from an API, VehicleFactory decides whether to build a Car, Motorcycle, or Truck, so I don't have new-statements and instanceof checks scattered around. Fifth, Builder for ParkingTicket, because tickets have several optional fields and a fluent builder reads far better than a telescoping constructor.

The key message is that each pattern prevents a specific maintenance problem — without Strategy, fee logic pollutes the lot; without Observer, the lot is tightly coupled to every board. And I'd be honest that I only apply a pattern when the problem is real. Using a Factory for a trivial two-class hierarchy just adds indirection. Naming the problem first and the pattern second is what separates a thoughtful answer from pattern-name bingo.

questions.question: How would you handle concurrent access to parking spots in your design?

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of race conditions in multi-threaded environments and ability to apply Java concurrency primitives to prevent data corruption in shared state.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Ignoring thread safety entirely or synchronizing the entire ParkingLot class, which creates a single bottleneck and destroys throughput when multiple vehicles park simultaneously.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain lock granularity trade-offs—locking individual spots versus entire floors—and mention performance implications like contention vs overhead, or discuss using AtomicReference with compareAndSet for lock-free updates.

questions.direct_answer: Use synchronized methods or ReentrantLock around the check-and-occupy operation to prevent race conditions. The critical section is when a thread checks if a spot is available and then marks it occupied—two threads could both see the spot as free and try to take it. Store parking spots in ConcurrentHashMap for thread-safe lookups. Use AtomicBoolean or volatile for spot status flags to ensure visibility across threads.

answer_sections.content: Concurrency is a real concern in a parking lot system — multiple entry barriers could assign the same spot simultaneously. The race condition is the classic check-then-act: both threads see occupied=false, both park, both think they succeeded. The fix: make the check-and-set atomic. I'd make tryPark() synchronized on the ParkingSpot, or better, use AtomicBoolean for the occupied flag and compareAndSet() for lock-free thread safety. The ParkingFloor's spot lookup also needs to be thread-safe — use ConcurrentHashMap instead of HashMap. For the interview, acknowledging this issue and describing the solution demonstrates production thinking, even if we're designing at the class level.

beats.text: AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false, true) atomically checks the current value and sets it — if two threads race, only one gets true back. The other gets false and must find a different spot.

production trap: don't synchronize at the ParkingLot level — that serializes all spot assignments across all floors, which kills throughput. Synchronize at the individual ParkingSpot level so different spots can be assigned concurrently.

sections.title: Concurrent Spot Assignment
sections.content:
Real lots have **multiple entry gates** = multiple **threads**. The danger is a **race condition** in the classic *check-then-act* sequence: two threads both read `spot.isFree() == true`, both proceed to park, and you've double-booked one spot.

The fix is to make **check-and-claim atomic** — one indivisible step. Java gives you `synchronized`, `AtomicReference.compareAndSet`, and concurrent collections. The skill being tested is **lock granularity**: lock the *spot*, not the whole lot, so different spots can be claimed in parallel.

sections.title: Race condition — check and act are separate
Atomic claim — check-and-set in one step
The Race vs the Fix
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["Gate 1 & Gate 2
both see spot free"] --> B{"Atomic
compareAndSet?"} B -- "No (check then act)" --> C["Both park
= double booking"] B -- "Yes" --> D["Only one wins
other retries elsewhere"] ```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Synchronizing the whole `ParkingLot`** — serializes all gates; kills throughput. Lock the spot, not the lot.
- **`HashMap` for shared spots** — `ConcurrentModificationException` under concurrent writes; use `ConcurrentHashMap`.
- **`ReentrantLock` without `try/finally`** — an exception leaves the lock held forever (deadlock). Always unlock in `finally`.
- **Treating check and act as two steps** — that gap is the race. Make it one atomic operation.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- The bug is a **check-then-act race**; the fix is an **atomic check-and-claim**.
- `AtomicReference.compareAndSet(null, v)` = lock-free claim; `synchronized park()` = lock-based, also fine.
- **Fine-grained locking** (per spot/floor) preserves throughput; lot-wide locks don't.
- Use **`ConcurrentHashMap`** for shared spot storage.
- With explicit locks, **always unlock in `finally`**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The concurrency problem is two vehicles at two gates trying to take the same spot at the same instant. Both threads check that the spot is free, both see true, and both park — that's a classic check-then-act race condition, and it double-books the spot. The fix is to make the check and the claim a single atomic operation so only one thread can win.

The simplest version is to make the park method on ParkingSpot synchronized, so only one thread enters at a time. A nicer, lock-free version uses an AtomicReference for the occupying vehicle and calls compareAndSet from null to the vehicle — if two threads race, exactly one gets true back and the other has to look elsewhere. For the collection of spots, I'd use a ConcurrentHashMap instead of a plain HashMap so reads and writes are safe.

The detail interviewers really want is lock granularity. A common fresher mistake is to synchronize the whole ParkingLot or the entire park method, which means only one car can park anywhere at a time and throughput collapses. Instead I lock at the spot level — or at most the floor level — so cars on different floors don't block each other. And if I use an explicit ReentrantLock, I always release it in a finally block, otherwise an exception mid-operation leaves the lock held and the system deadlocks. Even though we're designing at the class level, proactively raising this shows production thinking.
